**Summary.** This paper introduces Continuous-Process Randomized Compilation (CPRC) to extend error correction techniques from discrete quantum gates to continuous-time processes. Using the continuous process tensor (cPT) framework, the authors derive rigorous error bounds and prove convergence for systems interacting with memory-bearing environments. This offers a unified, quantitative toolset for designing robust quantum controls in realistic, non-Markovian settings.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous, unified theoretical framework for error mitigation in open quantum systems, moving beyond the limitations of discrete circuit models to address continuous-time memory effects crucial for realistic quantum hardware.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of extending Randomized Compiling (RC) from discrete gate operations to continuous-time quantum processes that interact with memory-bearing environments.

**Main result.** It derives a total-variation error bound for full adaptive output records and proves the convergence of trajectory-averaged continuous process tensor (cPT) coefficients for various bath types.

**Method.** The authors build the Continuous-Process Randomized Compilation (CPRC) framework within the cPT formalism, analyzing four specific random unitary control protocols.

**Model / system.** The system involves quantum processes described by the cPT, which unifies random unitary control trajectories, finite-duration instruments, and environmental dynamics. The analysis is tested using qubit models coupled to thermal Drude baths.

**Key observables.** Total-variation (TV) error bound, Operator Conditional Mutual Information (CMI), output probabilities, and two-particle coefficients.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The study examines various environmental characteristics, including Gaussian baths (like the Drude spectrum) and finite-dimensional non-Gaussian environments.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the cPT framework, which is an operational description, and assumes bounded centered coupling and mixing conditions for deriving error bounds.

**Figures summary.** The notes mention a detailed resolution audit (TABLE III) comparing CMI values across different protocols (Fixed, Brownian, OU) and varying computational parameters (time blocks, field rank).

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the cPT framework, proves theoretical results regarding covariance and error bounds, and concludes with numerical validation using qubit models and various bath types.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Traditional discrete randomized compiling (RC) tailors errors with random control frames at logical-gate boundaries, but fails to capture intra-instrument control evolution or persistent system-environment coupling. In memory-bearing environments, errors correlate across times, not just single gates. We build continuous-process randomized compilation (CPRC) in the continuous process tensor (cPT) framework, unifying random unitary control trajectories, pointwise-covariant finite-duration instruments, and environmental dynamics on one time axis. We study four protocols: fixed Pauli refresh, bounded Cayley paths, unitary Brownian motion, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck driving. We obtain three key results: (1) Pointwise covariance ensures each trajectory exactly reproduces the target logic without system-environment coupling; a closed-frame counterexample proves endpoint-only compensation causes first-order instrument errors. (2) Independent Pauli conjugations over full intervals diagonalize error histories at boundaries, but classical labels retain environment-induced correlations, confirmed by an exact static-bath solution. (3) We derive a total-variation error bound for full adaptive output records under bounded centered coupling and mixing conditions. We prove convergence of trajectory-averaged cPT coefficients in fixed particle sectors for finite non-Gaussian environments and Gaussian baths with time-integrable covariance, including the uncut Drude spectrum. We numerically validate the theory in a qubit model via output probabilities, operator conditional mutual information, and all two-particle coefficients for both qubit and thermal Drude baths. This work extends RC from discrete circuits to continuous-time memory-bearing quantum processes, offering a unified framework, quantitative tools, implementable schemes, and benchmarks for non-Markovian error tailoring.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper models traffic flow on complex networks using a two-queue system and compares two control protocols: Free Entry (FE) and Restricted Entry (RE). It demonstrates that the RE protocol acts as a superior self-regulating buffer, mitigating the severity of congestion and changing the jamming transition from abrupt to gradual, especially when external demand fluctuates periodically.

**Why it may be interesting.** The study of non-equilibrium dynamics, phase transitions (jamming), and the effect of external periodic forcing on collective behavior is directly relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and open quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates how regulating entry into a main flow queue, using a two-queue gate control mechanism, improves routing efficiency in complex networks subjected to periodic traffic fluctuations.

**Main result.** The restricted entry (RE) protocol significantly outperforms the free-entry (FE) protocol, particularly under large periodic fluctuations, by replacing sudden jamming transitions with gradual, continuous ones.

**Method.** The analysis uses macroscopic and microscopic modeling of traffic flow, comparing the dynamics of FE and RE protocols using order parameters and time-averaged system occupancy.

**Model / system.** The model simulates traffic movement on complex networks (like ER or BA graphs) using a two-queue system (waiting and flowing queues) at each node, driven by a time-varying external demand.

**Key observables.** Total system vehicles A(t), order parameter $\rho$ (congestion rate), and the critical transition point $p_c$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Periodic fluctuation amplitude $\eta$, driving period $T$, and the traffic-awareness parameter $h$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The approach relies on a simple local rule using only local queue information, making it highly implementable.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the temporal evolution of system occupancy $A(t)$ for both protocols under varying $\eta$, and phase diagrams showing the transition point $p_c$ dependence on $\eta$ for both FE and RE.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining the two-queue model and protocols (FE vs. RE) to performing macroscopic analysis of congestion transitions ($\rho$ vs. $p_0$), and finally analyzing the impact of periodic forcing ($\eta > 0$) on the stability and transition characteristics.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Traffic movement on highways and data packet transmission across the Internet serve as prototypical examples of collective dynamical behavior in complex systems. Although enhancing traffic flow in complex networks has been extensively investigated, most existing studies focus on single-queue models. In this paper, we introduce a simple yet effective two-queue scheme with gate control that regulates vehicle entry and integrates it with the routing protocol. When vehicles arrive at a on-ramp gate, they first join a waiting queue and are permitted to enter the main flowing queue once it has emptied. This two-queue strategy is especially advantageous when highway inflow varies periodically with large fluctuations, as is commonly observed in real traffic. Moreover, it modifies the system's failure characteristics, replacing sudden, discontinuous jamming transitions with gradual, continuous ones. The approach is based on a simple rule using only local queue information, making it easy to implement and widely applicable. Beyond the specific setup studied here, it can be applied to other transportation networks under different conditions or extended to other queuing systems, such as Internet data packet routing.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proves that quantum Gibbs samplers rapidly mix to the true thermal Gibbs state for 1D quantum spin chains at any temperature. The mixing time scales logarithmically with system size, $O(\log(n/\epsilon))$, and the required quantum circuit depth for state preparation is also polylogarithmic. This provides a powerful theoretical tool for simulating thermalization in quantum many-body physics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides rigorous, resource-efficient theoretical guarantees for simulating thermalization dynamics in quantum many-body systems, which is crucial for understanding quantum thermalization and equilibrium states.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to prove the rapid mixing time of quantum Gibbs samplers for 1D quantum spin chains at any finite temperature.

**Main result.** Rapid mixing is proven for the quantum block heat-bath dynamics in $O(\log(n/\epsilon))$ time, and the Gibbs state preparation can be done with $O(	ext{polylog}(n/\epsilon))$ quantum circuit depth.

**Method.** The analysis uses a path-coupling argument bounding the evolution in the quantum Wasserstein distance of order 1, combined with techniques for approximating quantum channels with efficient quantum circuits.

**Model / system.** The system is a 1D quantum spin chain on a periodic lattice ($\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$) governed by a nearest-neighbor Hamiltonian. The dynamics are simulated using a quantum block heat-bath process defined by a Lindbladian.

**Key observables.** Mixing Time ($t_{	ext{mix}}$), Quantum Wasserstein distance ($W_1$), and Quantum Circuit Depth.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Finite temperature ($eta$), system size ($n$), error tolerance ($\epsilon$), and constant block length ($\ell$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The Hamiltonian is assumed to have bounded local interactions, and the proof relies on establishing specific boundary estimates and Lipschitz control conditions.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 outlines the proof structure linking static properties to dynamical mixing. Table 1 compares the derived mixing time bound against other known results for spin systems.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the rapid mixing result using the quantum Wasserstein distance, followed by providing an explicit quantum circuit depth bound for state preparation. Later sections confirm the optimality of the logarithmic scaling for both periodic and open boundary conditions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We prove that a quasi-local quantum Gibbs sampler rapidly mixes to the Gibbs state of any 1D finite-range Hamiltonian at all finite temperatures in $\mathcal{O}\left(\log (n/\varepsilon)\right)$ time. Each update traces out a contiguous block of constant length and reconstructs it using the Petz recovery map, following early proposals for quantum heat-bath Gibbs samplers by Kastoryano and Brandão~\cite{kastoryano2016quantum}. Our proof directly bounds the distance between the updated state and the target Gibbs state using quantum Wasserstein distance of order $1$. We further provide $\mathcal{O}(\text{polylog}(n/\varepsilon))$ depth of quantum circuits to prepare these Gibbs states. We hope these techniques will facilitate the analysis and design of other Gibbs samplers.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes pulsar spin noise using a two-component model for a neutron star's rotation, distinguishing between models where total angular momentum is conserved (stationary) versus those where it diffuses (nonstationary). By developing Gaussian process methods, the authors show that joint observations of both the crust and superfluid components are necessary to robustly test the fundamental question of angular momentum conservation in these extreme astrophysical objects.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous application of Gaussian process methods to model complex, multi-component stochastic dynamics in a physical system like a neutron star provides a template for analyzing open quantum systems where multiple coupled degrees of freedom are involved.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central problem is testing the stationarity of pulsar spin noise, which is equivalent to determining whether the total angular momentum of a neutron star is conserved.

**Main result.** The authors show that the two-component model can be analyzed for both nonstationary (diffusive) and stationary (conserved) dynamics, and these models are fully testable using joint observations.

**Method.** The analysis develops scalable Gaussian process methods to construct and analyze the likelihood function for observing both the crust and superfluid rotational states simultaneously.

**Model / system.** The system is a two-component dynamical model of a neutron star's rotation, involving a crust component and a superfluid component, whose dynamics are governed by stochastic torques.

**Key observables.** Pulsar timing data (measuring the crust's rotational state) and continuous gravitational wave observations (inferred superfluid interior dynamics).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Relaxation time scale ($	au$), ratio ($r$), and various steady-state averages ($\langle\langle\alpha_cangleangle, \langle\langle\Delta\Omegaangleangle, Q_c, Q_s$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Robust inference is difficult if only one component (e.g., crust) is observationally accessible, and the analysis relies on the assumption of Gaussian noise processes.

**Figures summary.** Figure C3 shows parameter posteriors for singular Brownian motion, comparing fixed noise vs. joint state+noise estimation, and includes noise diagnostics for residuals.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the two-component model, derives the necessary Gaussian process methods, and then applies these methods to distinguish between the nonstationary (diffusive) and stationary (conserved) limits of the total angular momentum.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We present an analysis of pulsar spin noise based on physically-motivated two-component models of spin wandering. We focus on two models, distinguished by their total angular momentum dynamics: a singular, nonstationary model with a diffusive total angular momentum, and a minimal, stationary model anchored on a conserved total angular momentum. We develop scalable Gaussian process methods and, using mock data, show that the two models are fully testable and distinguishable with full-state observations, i.e., simultaneous independent data on the crust and the superfluid rotational states. This paves a path to testing stationarity in pulsar spin noise, potentially achievable with joint continuous gravitational wave observations and radio timing of pulsars. However, robust inferences and predictions are harder to achieve, and depend on the priors and data quality, when only one component is observationally accessible.

</details>

**Summary.** This work investigates a quantum Ising chain with complex anisotropic interactions to map out its phase diagram and dynamic critical points. By analyzing vector chiral order, entanglement entropy, and the Loschmidt amplitude, the authors demonstrate that the competition between different interactions leads to rich quantum phases and distinct dynamical critical behaviors. It highlights how off-diagonal exchange terms significantly enrich both the static and time-dependent physics of the quantum magnet.

**Why it may be interesting.** The paper provides a detailed study of how geometric frustration (dimerization) and anisotropic interactions enrich both the equilibrium phase diagram (chiral order) and the non-equilibrium dynamics (DQPTs), offering rich material for understanding quantum criticality beyond simple Ising models.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the emergence of vector chiral order and the nature of dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) in a quantum Ising chain subjected to dimerized anisotropic Gamma interactions.

**Main result.** The competition between Gamma anisotropy and the transverse field dictates the phase diagram, revealing distinct critical behaviors, including a gapless critical line in the absence of Ising interactions and periodic/aperiodic sequences for critical times.

**Method.** The analysis employs theoretical techniques including Jordan-Wigner transformation, mapping the system to a fermionic Hamiltonian, and utilizing the Loschmidt amplitude to probe non-equilibrium dynamics.

**Model / system.** The system is a transverse-field Ising chain incorporating dimerized anisotropic Gamma interactions. The Hamiltonian is analyzed using a Bogoliubov quasiparticle formulation, which is then used to calculate correlation functions and the Loschmidt amplitude.

**Key observables.** Vector spin chirality, vector chiral order parameter, spin-spin correlation functions ($C_{xx}^r, C_{xy}^r$), subsystem entanglement entropy ($S_L$), and the Loschmidt amplitude/rate function ($G(t), g(t)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Transverse field ($h$), Ising coupling ($J$), and the anisotropic Gamma interaction ($\Gamma$), along with the dimerization parameter ($\alpha$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the system starts in the ground state for DQPT calculations, and the fermionic representation is used to diagonalize the Hamiltonian.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the phase diagram based on chiral order, the closing of the energy gap ($\Delta=0$) defining critical lines, and the rate function $g(t)$ showing nonanalytic cusps marking DQPT critical times.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically explores the equilibrium phase diagram using chiral order parameters, analyzes correlation functions and entanglement entropy to characterize critical points, and finally uses the Loschmidt amplitude to independently probe DQPTs, comparing the results from both equilibrium and non-equilibrium diagnostics.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate a transverse-field Ising chain with dimerized anisotropic Gamma interactions and demonstrate that, both in the absence and presence of Ising interactions, the competition between Gamma anisotropy and the transverse field gives rise to vector chiral order and dynamical quantum phase transitions. The phase diagram comprises positive and negative vector chiral phases and a paramagnetic phase, characterized by the vector spin chirality and the vector chiral order parameter. In the absence of Ising interactions, we identify a gapless critical line that exhibits no finite-size drift, along which the spin-spin correlations and subsystem entanglement entropy display behavior distinct from that of Ising criticality. Furthermore, we find that the critical times of dynamical quantum phase transitions form periodic or aperiodic sequences, depending on the quench path. Our findings highlight how dimerized off-diagonal exchange enriches both equilibrium ordering and dynamical critical behavior in a quantum Ising chain.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper investigates the renormalization group flow of stochastic turbulence to determine if perturbative results can be reliably extrapolated to physical conditions. By calculating the exponent $\omega$ to high loop orders, the authors find evidence suggesting that the fixed point governing the system loses its real stability before reaching the physical forcing strength, implying a fundamental breakdown of the simple perturbative RG description.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical fluid dynamics, the methodology—using advanced RG techniques to probe the breakdown of perturbative expansions—is highly relevant to understanding non-equilibrium critical phenomena in quantum many-body systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates whether the perturbative Renormalization Group (RG) description of stochastic turbulence can be smoothly extended from small forcing parameters ($\epsilon \approx 0$) to the physically relevant large-scale forcing ($\epsilon_{	ext{phys}} = 2$).

**Main result.** The analysis suggests that the RG fixed point loses its reality or stability in an intermediate range of $\epsilon$, indicating a possible obstruction to a simple, controlled perturbative extrapolation to the physical regime.

**Method.** The authors employed advanced RG techniques, calculating the correction-to-scaling exponent $\omega$ up to five-loop order in the large-$d$ limit, and using pattern recognition (OEIS) to conjecture a closed-form expression for $\omega(\epsilon)$.

**Model / system.** The system modeled is homogeneous isotropic stochastic turbulence, governed by the Navier-Stokes equation driven by a Gaussian random force. The analysis is performed in the large spatial dimension limit ($d 	o \infty$).

**Key observables.** The correction-to-scaling exponent $\omega(\epsilon)$, the stability and reality domains of the RG fixed point, and the renormalized parameters ($
u_Z, g_0, Z_g, D_0$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The forcing parameter $\epsilon$, which varies from the perturbative limit ($\epsilon 	o 0$) to the physical limit ($\epsilon_{	ext{phys}} = 2$). The large dimension limit ($d 	o \infty$) is crucial for the calculations.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumptions include performing calculations in the large-$d$ limit and treating the derived closed-form expression for $\omega(\epsilon)$ as a conjecture based on observed coefficient patterns.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 is noted to show the conjectured closed-form expression for $\omega(\epsilon)$ and plots the stability and reality domains of the RG fixed point, highlighting the physical value $\epsilon_{	ext{phys}} = 2$.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by setting up the stochastic turbulence model via field theory, performing multi-loop calculations of the RG flow equations (determining $\omega$), conjecturing a closed form for $\omega(\epsilon)$, and finally analyzing the stability and reality of the resulting fixed point solution across the parameter space $\epsilon \in [0, 2]$.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We examine whether the perturbative renormalization group (RG) regime of stochastic turbulence can be continued from small $\varepsilon$ to the physical value $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{phys}}=2$, corresponding to large-scale forcing. Exploiting the simplifications of the large-$d$ limit, we calculate the correction exponent $ω$ to five-loop order and find a simple structure suggesting a closed analytic form. This form implies that the fixed point stable near $\varepsilon=0$ ceases to be simultaneously real and infrared stable before reaching $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{phys}}=2$, pointing to a possible change of infrared regime rather than a controlled perturbative RG extrapolation.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper analyzes the information content gained from measuring a weak absorber using single photons in an interferometer. It demonstrates that while negative quasiprobabilities are theoretically significant, they do not improve the information per absorbed photon in a single pass. True advantages are found either through phase accumulation over multiple passes or when the measurement setup is designed to exploit specific interference effects.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides rigorous theoretical bounds on quantum metrology, specifically quantifying when and how negative quasiprobabilities can enhance measurement sensitivity beyond classical limits in the context of photon loss.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the fundamental limits on the information gain per absorbed photon when performing interaction-free measurements on a weak sample.

**Main result.** For single-pass measurements, negativity does not improve the total information per absorbed photon; advantage only accumulates over multiple, uncounted passes or when the phase response is significant.

**Method.** The analysis uses the Fisher information derived from the linear response of output probabilities to weak absorption or phase shifts, utilizing negative Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobabilities.

**Model / system.** The system models a single photon passing through a $d$-path interferometer containing a weak absorber with transmittance $t$. The analysis extends to multi-pass scenarios using ring resonators.

**Key observables.** Fisher information ($F_s(t)$), evidence per absorbed photon ($\eta$), and the complex Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobabilities ($\varrho_C$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Transmittance $t$, number of passes $\ell$, and the weak value $\langle\hat{\Pi}(a)angle_w$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often relies on approximations, such as the Gaussian regime or small probabilities of absorption ($P(a)$).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the interferometer setup, showing how the single-shot gain ($R_M^{-1}$) decays for different measurement limits and how the gain is enhanced by negative weak values near null ports.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the single-pass bound using Fisher information (Theorem 1) to analyzing the role of negativity, and finally extends the analysis to multi-pass systems and the evidence gain ($\eta$) using advanced entropy measures.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Negative Kirkwood--Dirac quasiprobabilities are credited with the quantum advantage of interaction-free measurement and postselected metrology. We test that claim on the task interaction-free measurement was designed for: learning about a sample letting it absorb as little light as possible. The Kirkwood--Dirac distribution of path and output gives the linear response to a weak sample: its real part responds to absorption, its imaginary part to a phase. For a pure single photon passing once through any interferometer, the Fisher information about transmittance per absorbed photon is the direct-transmission value minus a sum of squared imaginary parts: no interferometer or readout beats direct transmission. Negativity plays no role beyond concentrating information in weakly lit outputs. The imaginary parts of the Kirkwood-Dirac distribution depend on the output basis here, not on the sample, so a basis exists in which every term is real, which is optimal. A single photon gains information per absorbed photon only through a phase response, which for an optical line needs a thick or inhomogeneously broadened sample, or through many passes when absorptions go uncounted, as shown by a critically coupled resonator. For detecting a weak absorber, negativity gives a single-shot advantage that does not accumulate over multiple trials; advantage instead accumulates when there are outputs which are dark without the object, a case which needs no negativity.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a transport theory for a Majorana interferometer incorporating edge vortex tunneling. It finds that while DC conductance is insensitive to topological effects, the low-frequency response reveals an effective capacitance sensitive to the non-Abelian statistics of the edge vortices. This provides a measurable diagnostic for topological physics in superconducting quantum devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** The focus on topological signatures (non-Abelian statistics) measurable via capacitance in a superconducting platform makes it highly relevant for understanding topological quantum computation pathways.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a transport theory for a generic two-arm co-propagating Majorana interferometer that incorporates both Majorana fermion tunneling and the effects of edge vortex (EV) tunneling.

**Main result.** While the DC conductance does not show signatures of edge-vortex interference, the interference manifests as an effective capacitance at low frequencies, which is sensitive to the non-Abelian anyon statistics of the edge vortices.

**Method.** The theory employs a replicated bosonization field theory framework to analyze the linear-response conductance tensor, generalizing previous treatments to asymmetric configurations.

**Model / system.** The system is a Majorana interferometer realized on a Topological Insulator proximitized by a Superconductor, featuring two co-propagating chiral Majorana edge modes and coupling points for both Majorana fermions and EVs.

**Key observables.** Effective capacitance ($C_{	ext{eff}}$) at low frequencies, and the frequency-dependent conductance tensor $G(\omega)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Thermal length $\ell_T = \hbar v / (\pi k_B T)$, and the degree of asymmetry in the interferometer arms ($\delta L$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the EV size is negligible compared to the thermal length $\ell_T$, and the theory is generalized to handle arbitrary length mismatches.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the schematic setup of the interferometer, showing the two chiral Majorana modes and tunneling processes involving EVs, and show color-scale plots of the finite-temperature DC conductance dependence on tunneling amplitudes.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from the initial Hamiltonian formulation (including Majorana and EV tunneling) to the application of a replicated bosonization framework to calculate the frequency-dependent conductance, distinguishing between DC and AC responses.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Co-propagating chiral Majorana edge modes are predicted to exist in proximity-coupled quantum anomalous Hall systems. They combine the exciting prospects of edge vortices as flying non-Abelian Ising anyons, with their fully electrical detection through anyon fusion processes. In this setup, electrical transport arises from the interference of a pair of Majorana edge states. By bosonizing the model with an additional replica sector, we generalize previous treatments to fully asymmetric configurations. We analyze a Mach-Zehnder interferometer and show that while the DC conductance does not exhibit signatures of edge-vortex interference, at low frequencies, this interference manifests as an effective capacitance. This quantity is sensitive to the non-Abelian anyon statistics of edge vortices and, in particular, carries signatures of their topological spin and nontrivial conformal dimension. We demonstrate that the thermal length $l_T = \hbar v/(πk_B T)$ is the relevant scale at low temperatures $T$, analogous to quasiparticle transport in conventional quantum Hall edge states with velocity $v$. As long as the interferometer arm lengths match within this length scale, transport signatures of the non-Abelian statistics of edge vortices remain visible.

**Summary.** This paper reports on the use of Additive Solid Immersion Lenses (SILs), fabricated via Pulsed Laser Deposition of high-k oxides like YSZ, to boost the light collection efficiency from NV centers in diamond. By mitigating total internal reflection losses, the technique significantly increases the measurable saturation intensity of the quantum emitter, making it a viable platform for quantum information processing.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the practical quantum optics challenge of coupling single-photon emitters to external optical circuits by engineering the local photonic environment, which is crucial for quantum networking and quantum memory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is the low photon extraction efficiency from shallow Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV−) centers in diamond due to total internal reflection losses caused by the refractive index mismatch with air.

**Main result.** The authors successfully demonstrated that using Additive Solid Immersion Lenses (SILs) made of high-k amorphous oxides significantly enhances light collection, achieving an average 63% increase in saturation intensity.

**Method.** The study combines numerical simulations (Monte-Carlo) to model photon extraction with experimental fabrication techniques like Pulsed Laser Deposition (PLD) and photolithography to create the SIL structures.

**Model / system.** The physical system is NV− centers embedded in diamond. The enhancement mechanism involves depositing high-k dielectric materials, such as Yttria-Stabilized Zirconia (YSZ), onto the surface to act as an immersion lens.

**Key observables.** Photon extraction efficiency ($\eta$), saturation intensity ($I_{sat}$), and the necessary laser intensity for saturation.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The refractive index ($n$) of the SIL material, the lateral offset ($\Delta$) of the light source, and the SIL geometry parameters (diameter $2r$, thickness $t$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Initial simulations did not consider Fresnel reflections, and the performance is sensitive to fabrication imperfections like sidewall deposition ('fencing').

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the fabrication process, showing the array of curved SILs and cross-sections, and compare fluorescence measurements (saturation counts) under different surface conditions.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from identifying the optical loss problem to simulating the theoretical enhancement using SILs, and finally validating the concept through the scalable, bottom-up fabrication and measurement of the enhanced photon collection efficiency.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy ($\mathrm{NV}^-$) defect in diamond can be used for quantum information processing via the readout of the radiative decay of the excited state into the ground state. The large refractive index mismatch of diamond and air causes low photon extraction efficiency due to total internal reflection losses. Here, we investigate the photon extraction numerically and report additive solid immersion lenses (SILs) consisting of the high-k dielectric yttria-stabilized-zirconia (YSZ) for surface modification and enhanced light extraction of shallow implanted nitrogen-vacancy centers. We demonstrate an average increase of 63% in saturation intensity using a scalable bottum up room temperature pulsed laser deposition and photolithography structurization process. The average necessary laser intensity for saturation is reduced by 33% by the SILs.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper demonstrates that adding local dissipation to the Bose-Hubbard model restores a robust, state-independent Lieb-Robinson bound, overcoming a major hurdle in analyzing bosonic quantum dynamics. By regularizing the state via photon loss, the authors prove that local approximations are valid uniformly in the initial state. This has significant implications for digital quantum simulation and quantum error correction codes.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a crucial theoretical tool—state-independent locality bounds—for bosonic systems, which is highly valuable for analyzing quantum simulation protocols and understanding information flow in complex quantum hardware.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of establishing operator-norm Lieb-Robinson bounds for bosonic lattice systems, which is difficult because information propagation velocity can depend on the local boson occupancy.

**Main result.** The authors prove that introducing local dissipation (on-site $\ell$-photon loss with $\ell>2$) restores an almost-ballistic Lieb-Robinson bound, allowing for uniform state-independent approximations.

**Method.** The core method involves using local dissipation to regularize the dynamics, allowing the use of Sobolev regularization techniques to bound the difference between the full and truncated evolution.

**Model / system.** The system is the Bose-Hubbard model on a lattice, described by a Lindbladian master equation incorporating on-site $\ell$-photon loss. Extensions cover cat-code dissipation and quartic bosonic models.

**Key observables.** Operator-norm local approximation estimates, Lieb-Robinson bounds, and the decay rate of the difference between full and restricted evolution.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dissipation order $\ell > 2$, the hopping coefficients $J_{ij}$, and the rates $\gamma_j$ are crucial parameters determining the bound's validity.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the existence of Sobolev-preserving and regularizing quantum Markov semigroups and the assumption of sufficiently strong local dissipation ($\ell>2$).

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from establishing the general difficulty of locality bounds in bosonic systems to introducing dissipation as a regularizing mechanism. It then proves the main Lieb-Robinson bound for the Bose-Hubbard model, extends this to cat-code dissipation, and concludes with applications like local adiabatic approximations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Closed bosonic lattice systems do not generally admit operator norm Lieb--Robinson bounds uniformly in the initial state. The reason is that the information propagation velocity can grow with the local boson occupancy, which can be macroscopically large. Here, we show that local dissipation restores an operator-norm Lieb--Robinson bound. We consider the dissipative Bose--Hubbard model described by a Lindbladian operator with on-site $\ell$-photon loss, $\ell>2$ and, for our main result, we establish an almost-ballistic Lieb-Robinson bound. Dissipation rapidly depletes highly occupied sites, thus regularizing the state on the Sobolev-type scale of local particle moments. The resulting moment bounds diverge as time approaches zero but remain integrable near zero at sufficiently low orders. We extend these ideas to treat cat-code dissipation and, for initial states in the code space, we prove a local adiabatic approximation uniform in the total volume. Further consequences include local channel approximation, a thermodynamic limit, and efficient digital quantum simulation. The point is that these applications are now available \textit{uniformly in the input state}, as for quantum spin systems, but in contrast to closed Bose--Hubbard systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper explores a profound mathematical triality linking stochastic growth models like TASEP, the DSSYK quantum field theory, and low-dimensional dilaton gravity. By showing these systems are mathematically equivalent in certain limits, the authors provide a unified, powerful framework for studying strongly coupled quantum phenomena. This work is significant for bridging non-equilibrium statistical mechanics with quantum gravity.

**Why it may be interesting.** The deep connections drawn between non-equilibrium statistical mechanics (ASEP/TASEP) and quantum gravity provide powerful, non-perturbative tools for understanding strongly coupled quantum systems, which is relevant for open quantum systems dynamics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the deep mathematical and physical connections, or 'triality,' between stochastic growth models, specific quantum field theories, and low-dimensional quantum gravity.

**Main result.** It establishes that the TASEP model is equivalent to the strong-coupling limit of 2D dilaton gravity, unifying these disparate fields under a single theoretical framework.

**Method.** The authors employ advanced techniques including deriving exact resolvent expressions, utilizing matrix integral representations, and establishing dualities between different physical models.

**Model / system.** The core models include the Totally Asymmetric Simple Exclusion Process (TASEP), the DSSYK model, and 2D dilaton gravity (related to JT gravity). These are connected via the KPZ universality class.

**Key observables.** Resolvent of the transfer matrix, cumulants, spectral densities, and partition functions.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Deformation parameter $q$, strong-coupling limit, and the coupling constant $\lambda$ governing the gravitational theories.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on identifying specific limits (e.g., strong coupling, $q 	o 0$) where the models simplify or become equivalent.

**Figures summary.** A flow chart is mentioned that schematically summarizes the connection between DSSYK, ASEP, TASEP, KPZ, Gravity, and Matrix models.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first defining the scope of the triality, then detailing the mathematical connections (Hamiltonian/transfer matrix coincidence), deriving specific results (resolvent), and finally unifying the interpretation through random walks and dualities.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We discuss the triality between stochastic growth models in the KPZ universality class, the DSSYK model, and low dimensional dilaton gravity. The TASEP model, which will be our primary focus, is identified with the strong-coupling limit of two-dimensional quantum gravity. The Hamiltonian of DSSYK and the transfer matrix of ASEP coincide up to an additive constant, and we derive the exact expression for the resolvent of the corresponding transfer matrix in ASEP on a finite interval. We also mention the relation of cumulants with the Tutte polynomial $T(1,q)$ of the crossing graph dual to the chord diagram, which implies the relationship of the models considered with the $Q=0$ Potts model coupled with gravity. We further exploit the realization of all these models in terms of different versions of discrete and continuous random walks on two-dimensional manifolds, which parameterize the Hilbert spaces of the respective theories. The representation of TASEP as the growth model of heaps provides new insight into strong-coupling gravity, suggesting its interpretation as an emerging phenomenon. The new dualities between ASEP and q-TASEP models and heap models providing a useful growth interpretation have been developed.

</details>

**Summary.** This work introduces the fermionic Gaussian Scrooge (fGS) ensemble to universally describe deep thermalization in free-fermion quantum systems. By analyzing the projected state after measurement, the authors prove that the ensemble converges to this specific Gaussian distortion, validating it for models like SYK2 and random Gaussian circuits. This provides a crucial theoretical tool for understanding quantum information scrambling in non-interacting fermionic settings.

**Why it may be interesting.** The concept of a universal ensemble describing thermalization in non-chaotic (free-fermion) systems provides a powerful, analytically tractable generalization of concepts from chaotic systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the theoretical description of deep thermalization in free-fermion systems following partial quantum measurements.

**Main result.** It establishes the fermionic Gaussian Scrooge (fGS) ensemble as the universal description for this process, proving its emergence for models like SYK2 and random Gaussian circuits.

**Method.** The authors use the replica trick and path integral methods, combined with a canonical purification technique, to calculate the moments of the projected quantum state ensemble.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on free-fermion systems, exemplified by the SYK2 model and random Gaussian circuits, where the evolution is governed by quadratic Hamiltonians.

**Key observables.** The projected ensemble moments ($ho_{PE}^{(k)}$), the correlation matrix ($\Gamma$), and the deviation from the fGS ensemble ($\Delta f_{GS}(k)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Evolution time ($t$), system size ($N$), and parameters defining the initial state (e.g., $p$ and $	heta$ for Gaussian circuits).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the system remaining Gaussian throughout evolution and utilizes the large-N expansion and saddle-point approximation for path integrals.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the schematic construction of the fGS ensemble, the path integrals and saddle-point solutions for SYK2, and numerical convergence plots showing the measured ensemble approaching the fGS prediction.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the fGS ensemble definition via purification, applies the replica trick to calculate projected moments for SYK2, and then confirms this universality numerically using random Gaussian circuits.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Measuring part of a many-body wave function generates a projected ensemble of pure quantum states on the unmeasured subsystem. Recent advances in deep thermalization have shown that, in chaotic systems, this ensemble universally converges to the maximally random ensemble compatible with its average density matrix, known as the Scrooge ensemble. By contrast, free-fermion systems are nonchaotic, and their quantum states are constrained to remain Gaussian. Motivated by this distinction, we introduce the fermionic Gaussian Scrooge ensemble to describe deep thermalization in generic free-fermion systems. This ensemble is defined as a distortion of the Gaussian Haar ensemble by the average density matrix, and its moments reveal an enlarged symmetry of Gaussian states in the replicated Hilbert space. We demonstrate the emergence of the fermionic Gaussian Scrooge ensemble in two complementary settings: (1) we analytically prove that the projected ensemble of the SYK$_2$ model follows the fermionic Gaussian Scrooge ensemble at arbitrary evolution times; (2) we provide numerical evidence that it emerges at sufficiently long times in random Gaussian circuits with charge conservation. Our results establish the fermionic Gaussian Scrooge ensemble as a universal description of deep thermalization in free-fermion systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This work investigates the quantum correlations within the vacuum state of a charged scalar field exposed to a time-varying electric field. By analyzing entanglement measures, the authors show that while total correlations increase, the usable entanglement decays to zero in finite time. This study connects non-perturbative particle production effects (Schwinger mechanism) to the dynamics of quantum information in curved or time-dependent backgrounds.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a concrete, non-equilibrium QFT example where quantum information measures (entanglement) decay due to external driving fields, linking particle creation (Schwinger effect) directly to quantum correlations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper analyzes how vacuum entanglement and quantum correlations evolve in a charged scalar field subjected to a time-dependent, homogeneous electric field.

**Main result.** The electric field increases state mixedness and total correlations, but the distillable entanglement decreases and vanishes at a finite time, demonstrating entanglement sudden death.

**Method.** The analysis employs canonical quantization, Gaussian state formalism, and the calculation of correlation measures like mutual information and logarithmic negativity.

**Model / system.** The system is a charged scalar field minimally coupled to an external, time-dependent electric field, studied in both (1+1) and (1+3) dimensional Minkowski spacetime.

**Key observables.** Mixedness of states, total correlations, distillable entanglement, mutual information, and logarithmic negativity.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Electric field strength ($E(t)$), pulse intensity, and the anisotropy angle ($\gamma$) relative to the field direction.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the Gaussian states formalism and assumes a spatially homogeneous external background field.

**Figures summary.** Figure 5 illustrates the anisotropy of the mutual information at t=0, showing dependence on the angle $\gamma$ between the electric field and the separation vector.

**Paper structure.** The paper reviews the field dynamics, details QI techniques for Gaussian states, applies these tools to QFT in Minkowski spacetime using local observables, and finally studies the time evolution and anisotropy using specific pulse profiles.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We analyze the correlations of the vacuum state of a charged scalar field by constructing localized observables in two disjoint regions. We consider a time-dependent homogeneous electric field and examine the time evolution of correlations by relating it with the particle-antiparticle creation through the Schwinger effect. Our results show that the electric field increases the mixedness of the states and enhances total correlations, while the distillable entanglement among the regions decreases, vanishing at a finite time for sufficiently intense pulses within the non-perturbative pair-production regime. We also discuss the effect of anisotropy induced by the external background, showing that the distribution of correlations acquires a nontrivial directional dependence.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper experimentally demonstrates that real-world QKD hardware leaks information about the transmitted quantum state via electromagnetic radiation. By measuring these emissions, the authors show that the transmitter is the main source of leakage, and the state-dependent signals allow for potential eavesdropping. The findings emphasize the critical need for robust physical shielding and hardware design to secure quantum communication networks.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work bridges the gap between the theoretical security of quantum protocols and the practical, physical layer vulnerabilities, which is crucial for designing robust quantum network hardware.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The physical implementation of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) nodes is vulnerable to side-channel attacks, specifically through measurable electromagnetic (EM) leakage.

**Main result.** The QKD transmitter was identified as the primary source of EM leakage, and distinct, state-dependent spectral differences were observed, suggesting that quantum states can be inferred from the leaked EM radiation.

**Method.** The study involved measuring EM spectra and waveforms at 0 m and 3 m distances using specialized antennas in an anechoic chamber, comparing measurements with and without EM shielding.

**Model / system.** The experiment utilized a prototype QKD device implementing a time-bin decoy-state BB84 protocol with Y and Z bases.

**Key observables.** EM spectra and waveforms, state-dependent spectral differences (especially at the third harmonic of the 1241.6 MHz clock), and the attenuation factor provided by EM shielding.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Measurement distances (0 m, 3 m), frequency bands (10–6000 MHz), and the average attenuation achieved by shielding (21.2 dB).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the observed EM differences are due to the quantum state being transmitted, and that the threat can be mitigated by proper EM shielding.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the QKD transmitter setup, the shielding effect by comparing emissions with and without the rack door closed, and the state-dependent EM spectra.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from identifying the theoretical vulnerability of QKD to presenting detailed experimental measurements of EM leakage from the transmitter, quantifying the state-dependent signals, and concluding with necessary physical countermeasures.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Actual quantum key distribution network nodes may be vulnerable to side-channel attacks such as electromagnetic leakage. In this study, we measured electromagnetic emissions from a prototype quantum key distribution device implementing a time-bin decoy-state BB84 protocol with Y and Z bases. We measured the electromagnetic spectra and waveforms at distances of 0 m and 3 m from the transmitter and receiver inside an anechoic chamber. The results showed that the transmitter was the primary source of electromagnetic leakage, and distinct differences were observed between the quantum states generated at the third harmonic of the 1241.6 MHz clock.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces the 'stationarity test,' a novel theoretical framework to reconstruct the Hamiltonian of a quantum many-body system using only samples of its thermal Gibbs states. It provides rigorous algorithms for both determining the interaction structure and estimating the coupling coefficients. By connecting this test to the Quantum Fisher Information, it offers a powerful tool for quantum machine learning in condensed matter physics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, data-driven theoretical tool to characterize the underlying physics (Hamiltonian) of complex quantum systems using only measurements of their thermal equilibrium or near-equilibrium states, which is highly relevant for simulating and understanding open quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is learning the unknown Hamiltonian interactions governing a quantum many-body system solely from samples of its thermal (Gibbs) states.

**Main result.** The authors introduce the 'stationarity test' as a rigorous framework to perform structure and parameter learning for lattice Hamiltonians, even when only metastable states are accessible.

**Method.** The method centers on the stationarity test, which measures the rate-of-change of local observables under the dynamics generated by a guessed Hamiltonian, linking this test to the Quantum Fisher Information.

**Model / system.** The system involves quantum many-body systems modeled by lattice Hamiltonians, $H = \sum h_\gamma P_\gamma$, whose thermal equilibrium states are the Gibbs states, $ho_H = e^{-eta H} / 	ext{tr}[e^{-eta H}]$.

**Key observables.** Local observables ($O$), the rate-of-change measured by the stationarity test ($	ext{Test}_i$), and the Quantum Fisher Information (FIG).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Inverse temperature ($eta$), system size ($n$), approximation error ($\eta$), and the locality/distance parameter ($\ell$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The framework assumes that the stationarity test yielding zero implies the guessed Hamiltonian is close to the true one, and it extends to using metastable states instead of true Gibbs states.

**Figures summary.** Not specified.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the stationarity test framework, details algorithms for structure learning from Gibbs states, and presents extensions for parameter learning using thermal metastable states, concluding with a refinement of the area law for these metastable states.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The task of learning the Hamiltonian interactions governing a quantum system, given samples of its thermal (or 'Gibbs') states, is a foundational question at the intersection of quantum learning theory and many-body physics. In this paper, we draw connections to the quantum Gibbs sampling literature to introduce a natural learning algorithm we call the stationarity test: which simply "guesses" the Hamiltonian, and measures the rate-of-change of local observables, under the associated detailed-balanced quantum Markov chain [CKG23]. We leverage the stationarity test to address the following applications:   1. To give the first learning algorithm for the underlying interaction graph, i.e. structure learning, of lattice Hamiltonians at all temperatures, given copies of their Gibbs states.   2. To give the first learning algorithm for the coefficients of a lattice Hamiltonian, given only copies of its thermal metastable states, modeled as the "local minima" of the free energy.   3. In addition, we present a refinement to the recent area law for thermal metastable states [BCV25], which holds in the thermodynamic limit.   Our learning algorithms are rigorous, time-efficient, and nearly sample-optimal in system size and accuracy. At a technical level, our arguments are based on new approximate locality and convexity properties for the quantum Fisher information of these Gibbs sampling algorithms.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops the theory of Floquet simulation, demonstrating how periodically driven quantum systems can efficiently mimic the dynamics of arbitrary time-independent Hamiltonians. It provides a constructive proof that for local lattice Hamiltonians, the required driving frequencies and interaction strengths scale polynomially with system size. This offers a theoretically superior and more experimentally feasible alternative to traditional analogue simulation methods.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous theoretical framework for engineering quantum dynamics using time-periodic driving, which is highly relevant for designing experiments with trapped ions or superconducting circuits where smooth, periodic driving is feasible.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper establishes a comprehensive theory for Floquet simulation, aiming to synthesize arbitrary time-independent quantum Hamiltonians using periodically driven (Floquet) systems.

**Main result.** It provides a constructive characterization showing that Floquet-universal Hamiltonians can simulate any Hamiltonian in their generated Lie algebra, with efficient scaling for local lattice Hamiltonians.

**Method.** The work uses advanced algebraic techniques, including analysis of the Magnus expansion and Lie algebra theory, to relate the effective time-independent dynamics to the driving parameters.

**Model / system.** The study analyzes quantum systems governed by time-periodic Hamiltonians, $H(t)$, comparing this to time-independent (analogue) and fully time-dependent (digital) simulation regimes.

**Key observables.** Quasi-energies, Floquet states, and the fidelity of simulation ($\epsilon$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The required local interaction strengths and the scaling of driving frequencies, which are shown to be polynomial in system size for local Hamiltonians.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the target Hamiltonian admitting a structure that allows for decomposition into commuting families of Lie polynomials, and that the generated Lie algebra is perfect.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the general theory of Floquet simulation power, then developing algebraic tools (like Lemma 55) to bound frequency coefficients, and finally applying these tools to prove efficient simulation theorems (Theorem 57) for $k$-local lattice Hamiltonians.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Analogue and digital Hamiltonian simulation represent two distinct approaches to making one quantum system replicate the physical properties of another, with consequences ranging from practical applications to complexity theory and quantum gravity. They are rooted in two distinct regimes of quantum dynamics: time-independent Hamiltonians for the former; fully controllable time-dependent quantum circuits in the latter. Time-periodic Hamiltonians represent an intermediate regime. In this work, we establish a theory of Floquet simulation where we use periodically driven Hamiltonians to synthesise time-independent ones.   We show that a set of interactions $S$ can Floquet-simulate every Hamiltonian in the Lie algebra $\mathrm{Lie}(S)$, and consequently we give a complete and constructive characterisation of Floquet-universal Hamiltonians that are able to produce any target Hamiltonian. Notably, our construction uses only $O(1)$ local interaction strengths and ratios thereof, avoiding the impractical multi-scale local interaction strengths often required in analogue simulation via time-independent Hamiltonians. Instead, the construction requires a range of driving frequencies which scales polynomially with system size for important classes such as $k$-local lattice Hamiltonians. This has immediate complexity-theoretic implications, including numerous BQP-completeness and QMA-hardness results for natural physical properties and quantities studied in Floquet physics.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work generalizes the fluctuation-dissipation theorem and Einstein relations to systems in rotating thermal equilibrium. By starting from the phase-space KMS relation, the authors derive new tensorial contributions and establish a novel link between spectral zero modes and transport coefficients. This provides essential microscopic constraints for modeling quantum matter under rotation, such as in the quark-gluon plasma.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work provides fundamental, model-independent equilibrium constraints for studying non-equilibrium phenomena in rotating quantum matter, which is crucial for understanding heavy-ion collision signatures.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper derives generalized fluctuation-dissipation theorems (FDT) and Einstein relations for vector fields in a system undergoing rotating thermal equilibrium.

**Main result.** It establishes a model-independent generalized Einstein relation and discovers a new Einstein-type relation linking spectral zero modes to the nonrotating drag coefficient, applicable to studying rotating quantum matter.

**Method.** The derivation starts from the exact phase-space Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (KMS) relation, generalizing it to include total angular momentum conservation, and then applying linear response theory.

**Model / system.** The theory applies to general many-body quantum systems, with physical relevance highlighted in the context of the quark-gluon plasma and heavy quarkonium polarization in highly vortical media.

**Key observables.** Generalized FDT, generalized Einstein relation, spectral zero modes ($\gamma_{ij}^0$), and orbital polarization ($\langle L_z angle_J$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Thermal vorticity ($\varpi_{\mu
u}$), low-frequency spectral information, and the nonrotating drag coefficient ($\eta^D$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The derivation assumes global equilibrium constrained by energy-momentum and total-angular-momentum conservation, and utilizes local approximations in the transport analysis.

**Figures summary.** Not specified by the notes.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by deriving the generalized FDT from the KMS relation, then obtaining the generalized Einstein relation, and finally applying these constraints to specific physical phenomena like quarkonium polarization and detailed balance.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We derive a generalized fluctuation-dissipation theorem (FDT) for vector fields in rotating thermal equilibrium from an exact phase-space Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (KMS) relation. The resulting FDT contains rotation-induced tensorial contributions beyond a scalar thermal factor. In the local transport limit, we obtain a model-independent generalized Einstein relation with rotation in which, through second order in thermal vorticity, symmetric momentum diffusion depends on low-frequency spectral information beyond that encoded in the rotation-dependent dissipative drag. Remarkably, we find a new Einstein-type relation linking zero modes in the spectral function to the nonrotating drag coefficient. These zero modes underlie a new mechanism for the orbital polarization of heavy quarkonium. The same FDT constraint yields a modified detailed-balance relation whose first-order vortical correction is governed by transition polarization, without explicit dependence on the bath model. Our findings establish microscopic equilibrium constraints for studying rotating quantum matter in various fields.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes the spectral behavior of strong turbulence on water surfaces, moving beyond simple weak-turbulence approximations. It predicts that the energy cascade leads to a strong-turbulence spectrum characterized by $\omega^{-4}$ and $k^{-4}$ dependencies. The work highlights that the transition to strong turbulence is governed by non-local interactions, making the resulting spectrum dependent on the initial energy pumping.

**Why it may be interesting.** The study of non-equilibrium energy cascades and spectral transitions in wave systems provides theoretical tools applicable to understanding energy dissipation and non-linear dynamics in complex physical systems, which shares mathematical structure with certain many-body relaxation processes.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the spectral characteristics of strong turbulence on water surfaces, focusing on the direct energy cascade of gravity waves.

**Main result.** The strong-turbulence spectrum is predicted to be $\langle|\eta_k|^2angle \propto k^{-4}$ and $\Psi(\omega) \propto \omega^{-4}$, suggesting the spectrum is not universal and depends on the pumping strength.

**Method.** The analysis combines weak-turbulence theory (Zakharov's approach) with renormalization group techniques to study the transition from weak to strong turbulence.

**Model / system.** The system is the surface of water undergoing strong turbulence, modeled using wave dynamics equations that account for gravity and wave interactions.

**Key observables.** Wavenumber spectrum $\langle|\eta_k|^2angle$, frequency spectrum $\Psi(\omega)$, and the critical balance parameter $\epsilon_k$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Pumping strength ($u$), peak wavenumber ($k_p$), and the transition scale $k^*$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the validity of weak-turbulence theory at low energy levels and examines the breakdown due to spectrally nonlocal interactions.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from reviewing the weak-turbulence theory for long waves to analyzing the transition to strong turbulence, deriving new spectral forms, and comparing the roles of gravity versus capillarity.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Here, I give a brief history of the theory, with twists and turns, and list possible predictions for the spectra of the direct cascade of gravity waves on the water. The description of long waves is straightforward within the weak-turbulence theory developed by Zakharov and his school. As the energy cascade proceeds to shorter scales, the mean surface steepness grows, and wave-breaking events appear with increasing frequency. Considering surface cusps, Phillips suggested a wavenumber spectrum (with a wrong magnitude, as I argue here) and a frequency spectrum whose whole form is incorrect. The right form for the frequency spectral slope due to breaking waves was suggested by Kuznetsov. Here we estimate the magnitude and argue that the frequency spectrum is expected to continue unchanged through the whole cascade. The transition from weak to strong turbulence in the wavenumber and spatio-temporal spectra is due to spectrally nonlocal interactions and happens earlier (at larger scales) than the dimensional estimate suggests. As a result, the magnitude of the strong-turbulence spectrum is not universal but depends on the pumping for a sufficiently long weak-turbulence cascade. The reason for nonlocality is likely that breaking of shorter waves is determined by the magnitude of the longest wave on whose crest they are running.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a resource theory to quantify measurement incompatibility preservability under noise. The authors prove that while noise can destroy this resource, they establish a no-go theorem against pre-filtering recovery but show that post-filtering can successfully activate the resource. This provides a practical guide for exploiting incompatibility in quantum information protocols.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a rigorous, quantitative framework (resource theory) for understanding how fundamental quantum correlations, like measurement incompatibility, are degraded by noise and how they might be recovered or utilized.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the fundamental quantum resource of measurement incompatibility and how its preservation degrades under noisy quantum channels.

**Main result.** They establish a no-go theorem showing pre-filtering cannot activate incompatibility, but demonstrate that post-filtering can stochastically activate such channels.

**Method.** The authors develop a resource theory framework, introducing robustness-based monotones, and utilize semidefinite programming (SDP) and iterative algorithms (seesaw) to quantify these properties.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on quantum channels ($\mathcal{N}$) acting on quantum systems, characterized by measurement assemblages ($\{M_a\}_{a,x}$), and the concept of measurement incompatibility.

**Key observables.** Measurement Incompatibility, Resource Monotone $R_{	ext{JIMIP}}(\mathcal{N})$, Quantum Steerability.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Noise strength ($t$), channel parameters (e.g., amplitude damping parameter $p$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on reformulating the resource measure using the Choi–Jamiolkowski isomorphism and assuming the equivalence between steering and measurement incompatibility.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the schemes for IA channels and numerically compare the preservation/activation of incompatibility using pre-filter only, post-filter only, and combined pre-post-filter operations.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the resource theory, defines the monotone $R_{	ext{JIMIP}}$, proves its properties (Faithfulness, Monotonicity), establishes the no-go theorem for pre-filtering, and finally demonstrates activation via post-filtering.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Measurement incompatibility is a fundamental quantum resource that enables advantages in many quantum information tasks, including cryptography and communication. However, unavoidable interactions between a system and its environment can degrade or even completely destroy measurement incompatibility; such a process is referred to as a measurement-incompatibility-annihilating channel. Recently, the capability of noisy quantum dynamics to preserve measurement incompatibility has been characterized within the resource theory of measurement incompatibility preservability. This motivates studying how to purify the preservation of measurement incompatibility and how to activate it from a measurement-incompatibility-annihilating channel. To this end, we first introduce our figures of merit as robustness-based resource monotones within this resource theory. We demonstrate that while pre-filtering operations can strengthen measurement incompatibility preservability, they cannot activate it from an incompatibility-annihilating channel, establishing a no-go theorem. Furthermore, we explicitly demonstrate that an incompatibility-annihilating channel can be stochastically activated via post-filtering operations. Our results provide a practical framework for exploiting measurement incompatibility in quantum information processing.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes quantum impurity models, showing that while calculating equilibrium properties like ground energy is classically tractable in polynomial time, simulating the system's time evolution is computationally hard (BQP-complete). The authors achieve this by developing specialized algorithms that exploit the structure of the fermionic bath excitations.

**Why it may be interesting.** The demonstration that a physical quantum system's dynamics can realize a universal quantum processor is highly relevant for understanding quantum simulation capabilities and computational complexity boundaries.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the computational complexity of calculating various properties (ground energy, thermal equilibrium, and dynamics) for quantum impurity models.

**Main result.** It establishes a sharp contrast: equilibrium properties can be efficiently approximated classically, while the time evolution simulation is proven to be BQP-complete.

**Method.** The authors develop specialized algorithms exploiting the exponential suppression of multi-particle bath excitations using energy-scale and Krylov depth basis organization.

**Model / system.** The system is a quantum impurity model, consisting of a small interacting subsystem (impurity) coupled to a large bath of free fermions, described by a Hamiltonian $H = H_0 + V$.

**Key observables.** Ground energy ($E_1(H)$), Helmholtz free energy ($F_eta$), and the time evolution operator ($e^{-iHt}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Accuracy parameters ($\epsilon$, $\delta$), inverse temperature ($eta$), and the size of the impurity ($m$, assumed constant).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The impurity size $m$ is assumed to be fixed and constant for the strongest complexity results.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the complexity for ground energy (Theorem 1.1), thermal equilibrium (Theorems 1.2-1.4), and finally proves the BQP-completeness of the time evolution simulation (Theorem 1.5).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

A quantum impurity model describes a small interacting subsystem embedded into a large bath of free fermions. Here we study the computational complexity of calculating the ground energy, thermal equilibrium, and dynamical properties of these models. Our work reveals a sharp contrast: equilibrium properties can be efficiently approximated by classical means, whereas time evolution can implement a universal quantum computation. More precisely, let $H$ be the Hamiltonian of an impurity model with $n$ fermionic modes and a constant-size impurity. We show that: (1) the ground energy of $H$ can be approximated to additive error $\varepsilon$ by a classical algorithm with runtime $\textsf{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon)$, improving on the quasi-polynomial runtime of the best previously known algorithm; (2) at inverse temperature $β$, the Helmholtz free energy and a classical description of the thermofield double state can be computed to precision $\varepsilon$ in time $\textsf{poly}(n,β,1/\varepsilon)$; (3) simulating the time evolution $e^{-iHt}$ is $\textsf{BQP}$-complete, for $H$ that is time-independent and has a fixed, constant impurity size. Our algorithms exploit exponential suppression of multi-particle bath excitations in a basis organized by energy scale and Krylov depth. Our universality construction realizes a stationary quantum processor whose program arrives in a stream of freely propagating fermions.

</details>
